item.title: I Spent $184 on Chakra Crystals and Tracked Everything for 60 Days
item.author: Kui Luo
item.content:encoded:
Quick background so you know where I'm coming from: I'm a backend developer who builds small SaaS tools for a living. I trust logs more than feelings. If something claims to work, I want a before-and-after number. Six months ago, crystals were firmly in the same mental category as horoscopes for me — fun at parties, useless in production.Then my sleep fell apart.Not "I stayed up late coding" falling apart. I mean lying awake at 2 a.m. with my heart doing drum solos, checking my resting heart rate on a $30 fitness band and watching it sit at 78 bpm when my baseline had been 61. Three side projects, two clients, one very patient girlfriend, and exactly zero downtime. My doctor used the word "stress" four times in a single appointment.Around that time my girlfriend left a black tourmaline stone on my nightstand. No lecture, just "try holding it when your brain won't shut up." I rolled my eyes, and then — because I'm incapable of trying anything casually — I turned it into a 60-day experiment with a spreadsheet. Here's the honest data, including the parts that made me uncomfortable.
The setup, so you can repeat it I didn't want to rely on vibes, so: No stones at all. Just tracking. five 9-day blocks, each focused on one "chakra" area, using only that block's stones. time to fall asleep (fitness band estimate plus my own note), resting heart rate, and a 3-line journal entry every night. Mood, anything weird, one line about work stress. $200. I ended at $184.37.I also did two things I'd recommend to anyone: I never changed my caffeine intake (2 coffees before noon, always), and I never decided on a "success number" in advance. I just wrote down what happened.
Block 1: grounding stones Stones: hematite, black tourmaline. Cost: $23.The pitch behind these is "grounding" — calming the racing-thoughts loop. I read the root chakra crystal guide on SagStone mostly to figure out which stones were even supposed to do what, and it's honestly more thorough than the Etsy listings I'd been squinting at.Results: average time to fall asleep went from 41 minutes (baseline) to 28 minutes. Resting heart rate: 74 → 70. My journal from day 19 says "held the rock for like 5 min before bed, felt ridiculous, slept anyway."Now, is that the rock or the ritual of lying down with no phone for five minutes? I genuinely can't tell you. Hold that thought.
Block 2: creativity stones Stones: carnelian, orange calcite. Cost: $19.This block was for the "I can't start writing this feature" problem. The sacral chakra stones guide frames these as creativity and emotional-flow stones.Honest result: I procrastinated exactly the same way (an average of 47 minutes of "quick checks" before deep work, per RescueTime). The one difference: I journaled more freely that week — longer entries, more honest ones. Maybe the carnelian on my desk made journaling feel like less of a chore. Or maybe orange rocks are just nice to look at. I kept two of them on the desk anyway. Judge me.
Block 3: confidence stones before the biggest pitch of my year Stones: citrine, tiger's eye. Cost: $31.Timing was luck — day 37 landed two days before the most important client pitch I'd ever given. The solar plexus chakra guide describes these as confidence stones, and look: I'm not going to pretend a yellow rock closed a $9,000 contract. What I noticed is that I showed up calmer than usual. Pre-pitch resting heart rate: 82, versus 95+ before similar calls in the past.My working theory: the stone gave my nervous system a specific physical thing to do with my hands and breath, instead of doom-refreshing my inbox. That's worth $31 even if it's pure placebo with good marketing.
Block 4: the one that actually surprised me Stones: rose quartz, green aventurine. Cost: $27.This is the block I expected to be pure nonsense — heart chakra stones for, quote, "love and emotional healing." I mostly did it for completeness.But my journal that week has three separate entries about arguments with my girlfriend that de-escalated instead of escalating. Count of actual fights in the 9-day block: 1. The 9 days before: 4. And no, the pitch win doesn't explain it — the win came a week earlier, and historically good weeks make us fight MORE, because I get insufferable.My best non-magical explanation: I already had a nightly wind-down ritual by then, and she joined it sometimes. Ten quiet minutes in the same room does more for a relationship than any stone. But the rose quartz is what got us into the room. Fine. Point taken, universe.
Block 5: sleep, round two Stones: amethyst, lepidolite. Cost: $34.Amethyst is THE sleep crystal according to every list on the internet. By this point my sleep was already much better (22-minute average to fall asleep), so this block was a "can it hold the gains" test.It held. 24-minute average, no breakthrough, no regression. My band's sleep score for the final week: 84, up from a baseline of 63.
The uncomfortable conclusion If you came here for "crystals are fake" or "crystals changed my life," you'll be disappointed: the rocks are probably placebo, and the placebo still outperformed my previous coping mechanism, which was scrolling Hacker News at 1 a.m.What I think actually happened: crystal healing works as a ritual scaffold. The stone is a physical prompt that says "the day is over now." Five minutes of sitting still with a rock beats five minutes of a phone screen, and it compounds. Would plain meditation with no rock have worked as well or better? Probably. But I never managed to build a meditation habit in 4 years of trying, and I built this habit in 60 days because the rock gave it a handle.Skeptics: we won. The mystical claims are unfalsifiable and I'm not defending them. But if a $184 pile of rocks is the entry fee to a working wind-down routine for an overworked developer, I've paid more for worse software.
If you want to try this without getting scammed Hard-won advice, take it or leave it:Cap your spend at $50 for a first kit. Everything I used cost under $40 per block, and the cheap stones worked as "well" as the pretty ones. The beginner's crystal healing guide on SagStone has a sane starter list — that's where I'd point a friend, instead of some $90 "supercharged bundle."Buy from shops with real, individual photos. Dyed glass sold as amethyst is everywhere. If a shop can't tell you the stone's origin region, skip it. Mine was time-to-sleep. If you can't name your metric, you're buying decoration, not running an experiment.Skip anything over $50 with healing claims attached. It's the same rock."Cleansing" costs nothing. Water, moonlight, done. Anyone selling you a $25 cleansing kit is selling you moonlight.Six months later, here's what's still true: I sleep around 7 hours, my resting heart rate is back to 63, and there are eleven rocks on my desk that my coworkers absolutely roast me for. I can't prove the rocks did anything mystical. I can prove that on day 1 I couldn't fall asleep before 1 a.m., and today I can't stay awake past 11.Whatever that's worth to you, it was worth $184.37 to me.

item.title: A language for humans and computers: Crystal in the AI era
item.author: Marvin Ahlgrimm
item.content:encoded:
At Rails World 2026, DHH described a division of labour that caught my attention: let agents write Rust and enjoy the result without having to look at the code.I can see the appeal, and I see the same sentiment at my workplace. When an agent writes the code, the effort of writing it by hand matters less. The compiler can catch mistakes as the agent works.But I still need and want to understand the software I am responsible for. For me, that points to Crystal.
Familiar syntax, static checks That familiarity matters even when I am no longer typing every line. I still read the implementation, question its choices and make changes myself. Type inference keeps many annotations out of the way while the compiler checks how values are used.Static checks on nullable values are available in other languages, too. What interests me about Crystal is having those checks in code I find straightforward to read. The agent gets feedback from the compiler; I get an implementation I can work with.
A compiler cannot choose the right tools How do I know the agent chose the right libraries and integration approach?Later in the talk, around 32:15, DHH describes assigning work asynchronously and reviewing the result. In my projects, that review includes the choices inside the implementation.I recently tried setting up a small Marten application with only one prompt. During implementation, I had to correct the agent twice:I wanted Marten Turbo and Marten Stimulus. The agent used npm to install the JavaScript packages instead of the CLI provided by Marten-importmap, which was the integration approach I wanted.It started developing its own throttling middleware instead of using Marten-throttle.I maintain these Marten shards, so I recognised the detours. npm was not the setup I wanted, and the custom middleware would have given me more code to maintain. Neither choice was a type error. Correcting them took knowledge of the project and its libraries.
Where compiler feedback has helped me A few months ago, when the models I used were less capable, I repeatedly saw compilation errors in generated Crystal code. Some involved incorrect handling of values. In some cases, compiler feedback led the agent towards a correction without me having to explain the type problem myself.A small example shows what the compiler can catch:The first argument might be missing. Its type is , also written . Calling directly is rejected because does not provide that method.An ordinary conditional handles the missing value:Inside the branch, the compiler knows the local variable cannot be . Crystal documents this type narrowing and its limitations, including why repeated getter calls cannot always be narrowed in the same way.Writing another / can feel tedious. I appreciate it more when an agent writes the code: I can see what it decided to do when the argument is missing.
Compiling still leaves a decision open There is another way to get past the error:This compiles, but raises an exception when the argument is missing. The standard-library documentation describes that behaviour and recommends avoiding where possible.Ameba's rule flags the assertion in this example. With the rule enabled, the linter gives the agent feedback about a shortcut the compiler accepts.The requirement is still open. Should a missing name produce a guest label? Should it stop the operation? Is absence supposed to be impossible? The compiler accepts both the guest fallback and the assertion. I still have to decide which matches the requirement.I still need end-to-end checks in both Marten applications and fixes or features for Meridian, my deployment tool. Parts of that work can already be automated, but the agents I use do not reliably cover all my requirements.Code and tests generated from the same misunderstanding can agree with each other.
Libraries and compiler feedback The Marten experiment showed that I cannot assume the agent will find the libraries I want. In a smaller ecosystem, I need to name them and provide current documentation.Waiting for the compiler also adds up. Long development builds slow down every round of corrections.The Generative Compilation preprint explores compiler feedback during the generation of partial Rust programs and reports improvements over feedback after complete generation. Its results suggest that the timing of compiler feedback matters as well as the checks themselves.I have not benchmarked my Crystal workflow against Rust. If you work with Rust every day, you may find its code easier to review.Crystal can be hard to read, too. Complex macros can hide what the code does, and its unsafe operations need careful review. I have to account for that effort even when an agent handles the implementation.
The code I still want to understand I expect agents to do more implementation work. In my projects, I still need and want to judge the result, check requirements and understand enough to make changes.With Crystal, static feedback helps the agent correct certain mistakes, and its syntax helps me inspect the decisions that remain.Crystal calls itself a language for humans and computers. As computers take on more of the writing, the human side becomes a reason to choose it. I want to delegate implementation and remain capable of understanding and changing the result. Crystal makes that practical for me.
